draft.title: Technology and living standards
card: After 1945, many new products became common in homes in countries like Australia. They included cars, televisions, washing machines, refrigerators and, later, computers.
Work
Machines and appliances cut the time spent on housework. Computers later changed office work, and many jobs came to need new skills.
Shopping
Cars let families live further from town and shop less often. Refrigerators let them store food for longer. Large stores such as supermarkets and shopping centres grew.
Free time
Television gave families a new way to spend evenings at home. Cars made it easier to take trips and holidays.
draft.remember: New products after 1945 changed how people worked, shopped and spent their free time.

a.q: In the 1950s, Lena's family in Ballarat buys a refrigerator. How does it change how the family shops?
opts: They can store food longer and shop less often
They must shop every day for fresh food
They stop buying food from shops at all
They can only buy food that is tinned
a.why: A refrigerator keeps food fresh for longer, so the family can make fewer trips to the shops. The idea that they must shop daily is wrong, because that was more common before home refrigeration.
a.clue: Think about what a fridge does to food.

b.q: Which change after 1945 shows how cars altered daily life in a city like Melbourne?
opts: More families lived far from the centre and drove to shops
More families gave up shopping for food altogether
More families spent evenings watching a home television
More families used computers to do their office work
b.why: Cars let people live further from town and travel to shops by road. Television and computers also changed life, but they changed free time and work, not how far people lived from shops.
b.clue: Which option is about cars, not another product?

a.best: They can store food longer and shop less often

b.best: More families lived far from the centre and drove to shops

problems.detail: The wrong options use absolutes ('must', 'only', 'at all'), while the right option alone uses the card's 'can'. A student can eliminate the distractors without knowing the idea.
The clue 'Which option is about cars, not another product?' rules out the computer and television options. The right answer is the only option that mentions driving, so the clue gives it away.

card: After 1945, many new products became common in homes in countries like Australia. They included cars, televisions, washing machines, refrigerators and, later, computers.
Work

proposal.remember: New products after 1945 changed how people worked, shopped and spent their free time.

a.q: In the 1950s, Lena's family in Ballarat buys its first refrigerator. What change to their shopping is most likely?
opts: Fewer trips to the shops, as fresh food keeps longer
More trips to the shops, as the fridge fills up quickly
More tinned food, as fresh food spoils in a fridge
The same trips as before, as a fridge does not keep food
a.why: A refrigerator keeps fresh food from spoiling for longer, so the family can buy more at once and shop less often. More trips is the reverse of this: shopping often for fresh food was more common before home refrigeration.
a.clue: Think about what a fridge does to fresh food.

b.q: After 1945, more families in Melbourne bought a car. Which change to daily life does this best explain?
opts: Families lived further out and drove to large stores
Families moved closer to town to be near small shops
Families shopped more often at a nearby corner store
Families took fewer trips away and stayed home more
b.why: Cars let families live further from town, shop less often and drive to large stores such as supermarkets. Moving closer to town or shopping more often at a corner store is the reverse of this, as those habits suit families without a car.
b.clue: What does a car let a family do about distance?

a.best: Fewer trips to the shops, as fresh food keeps longer

b.best: Families lived further out and drove to large stores
